items.e: ** Which Places Are Considered Enclosed for Dwelling, 14 Seifim:** Regarding every enclosed area that is not enclosed as a dwelling place, like a garden, an orchard, or a shed, but is just enclosed to protect its contents, the Sages forbade carrying something more than four amot in them if it is more than two seot. However, if it is two seot big, which is seven amot and four tefachim by seven amot by four tefachim, it is permitted to carry within it, whether it is square, round, long, or wide, as long as its length is not more than twice its width. If it is enclosed for dwelling, even if it includes a few mils, it is permitted to carry within all of it. Rema: And see below chapter 401 regarding whether generic cities are enclosed for dwelling. There are some who say that generic porches are enclosed for dwelling, because generally they are built and then enclosed (Mordechai Chapter Osin Pasin). And there are furthermore those who say that any porch attached to the house is considered enclosed for dwelling, because such was his intention (Hagahot Oshr"i on Chapter 2 of Eiruvin), and some disagree (Beit Yosef in the name of the Tosafot).

What is considered enclosed for dwelling purposes? If someone built a house or an opening from his house and then enclosed the area. If it was enclosed not for dwelling and one wants to enclose it for dwelling, he doesn't need to destroy the whole wall. Rather, he should make a breach bigger than ten [amot], and then the house will be open to a non-enclosed area. Then he can return and patch up the whole wall or just leave ten open and that ten is considered an opening. This way, it was open and is now enclosed [newly, and considered enclosed for dwelling]. If he breached one amah and then patched it, and then breaks an adjacent amah and patches it, and so on until he gets to ten, this is permitted. Rema: If it is difficult for him to break the wall, some say that he can put dirt next to the wall from both sides until the wall becomes less than ten [tefachim] tall and the width of the dirt is from four amot [up] for the length of ten amot along the wall. If the dirt is not ten [tefachim] tall, it will be as if he broke the wall, because there are not ten tefachim above the ground, and it is considered the ground of the yard. Even if he returns and removes the dirt, because it was nullified for one Shabbat, [it still holds]. Some disagree, claiming that dirt does not cancel [a wall's legal status] unless one will not ever remove it (Trumat HaDeshen chapter 75, and the Ros"h first chapter of Sukkah).
A piece of land raised ten [tefachim] is considered an enclosed space [not enclosed for dwelling].

If in an enclosure bigger than two seahs, trees are planted to reduce its area, there is no legal reduction (even if they are ten tall and four wide (the Magid chapter 16)), and this is also the case for one who digs a hole.
If one builds a column in order to legally reduce the area and the column is three tefachim wide, the area is effectively lessened.

If one builds a wall for ten [amot] in front of the original wall in order to nullify it as if it did not exist and therefore the area is enclosed for dwelling by the second wall, and the the new wall is three tefachim from the old one, this is permitted.

If one puts mud in front of the original wall in order to lessen the area of the enclosed space and the mud is thick enough such that if the wall is removed, it can stand on its own, the lessening is effective. If this is not true, there is no lessening.

If one builds a wall on top of the original wall in order to enclose it for dwelling, this is doesn't work. However, if the lower walls sink and the top walls remain, they now permit [carrying within the enclosed space]. However, if a hill is bigger than two seahs and someone makes a wall on its edge for dwelling, this works, because he lives in the space of the walls made now.

If an area enclosed for dwelling is bigger than two seahs and one plants trees in most of it, even if they are not planted in lines, they do not cancel the dwelling status of the area. However, if crops are planted in a majority of the area, the plants nullify its status as a dwelling place even if they are only two seahs. If a minority of the land has been planted and it is only two seahs, it is permitted [to carry within it]. If the area planted is more than two seahs, it is forbidden.

If someone has a garden in his yard and it is most of his yard, even if it is only two seahs, he may not carry from the garden or from the yard to the house. If it is bigger than two seahs, he can only carry in the garden and the yard within four amot. If it is the minority of the yard, if it is more than two seahs, the whole yard is forbidden [with regards to carrying]. If it is two seahs or less, it is forbidden to remove something from [the garden] to the house.

If an enclosed space bigger than two seahs is enclosed for dwelling and water enters it, if the water is drinkable, it does not nullify its status as a dwelling place, even if the water spreads more than two seahs and is very deep. If the water is not drinkable, it is treated like plants, assuming that it is ten tefachim deep.
If an enclosed space is three seahs big and it has a roof for one seah of that, it is permitted [to carry in the space] even if the roof is slanted.

If an enclosed place exactly two seahs big is adjacent to a yard and the barrier breaks, the enclosed place is forbidden [regarding carrying within it] because the place of wall adds to it, making it more than two seahs.

If an enclosed space is bigger than two seahs and is not enclosed for dwelling and an opening more than ten [amot] is made and then enclosed such that the new wall makes it permitted [to carry within the space] because the original wall that wasn't for dwelling is nullified, and later the new wall falls, it goes back to being forbidden.

1. **The Law of an Open Area Behind the House:** If an open area behind the house is bigger than two seahs and is not enclosed for dwelling, we only carry in it within four amot. If he made an opening from his house and afterwards surrounded the area [with walls], even if there is a threshingfloor between the area and the house it is considered enclosed for dwelling. RAMA: We are not careful regarding carrying in the yards behind houses because in this time, generic areas are enclosed for dwelling, as was explained above regarding enclosed spaces (his opinion).

**Surrounding partitions for Shabbat. 3 sections:** An individual who spent Shabbat in an open field and surrounded himself with inferior partitions — such as only vertical elements without horizontal, or only horizontal without vertical — up to two se'ah it is permitted to carry throughout; beyond two se'ah one may only carry within four cubits. The same law applies if there are two people. If there are three Jews they are considered a caravan and it is permitted to carry throughout even if the enclosed area is very large, provided they do not enclose more than they need — meaning there should not remain an empty two se'ah area that they do not need for use. But if there does remain an empty two se'ah area, one may only carry within four cubits throughout the enclosed space. This applies when they enclosed more than six se'ah; but if they did not enclose more than six se'ah, even if there is an empty two se'ah area, since there are three people it is permitted. Rema: A non-Jew does not combine to make a caravan, and some say the same applies to a minor. (Rambam ch. 11)

If there were three people who enclosed exactly what they needed and one of them died on Shabbat, they are permitted for the entire Shabbat, since Shabbat began in a state of permissibility. If there were two people who enclosed more than two se'ah and others joined them on Shabbat, it is forbidden, since Shabbat began in a state of prohibition.

If there were three people and each one enclosed his own area side by side and they made an eruv together — if the outer ones are wide and the middle one is narrow, such that the middle one is fully open to the outer ones and the outer ones have walls extending beyond it on each side — they are given their full needs in the middle one even if it is very large, since we view it as if they all dwell within it and there are three together. And also in the outer ones they are given their full needs, since having become a caravan in the middle one, the others are treated as a courtyard to the middle one. Some say the outer ones are only permitted up to two se'ah, and if one of them is more than two se'ah the middle one is also forbidden since it is fully open to it. If the outer ones are fully open to the middle one and the middle one has walls and there is one person in each — each one is only given two se'ah, and if one of the outer ones is more than two se'ah only that one is forbidden; but if the middle one is more than two se'ah the outer ones are also forbidden since they are open to a forbidden area. But if there is one person in each outer one and two in the middle, or two in each outer one and one in the middle — the two outer ones are given their full needs, as everything in the middle is considered as if it were in the outer ones. This applies when they are not open to each other by more than ten handbreadths, for if they are it constitutes a breach and even the walled areas are forbidden. All of this applies when the walls of the smaller one enter into the larger one, and when the walls of the smaller one are set back three handbreadths from the lengthwise walls of the larger one — for then the larger one restricts the smaller one (see above §374:3); otherwise it would appear protruding from outside yet flush from inside and would be treated as a lechi, and all would be considered walled and as if none of them is breached into the other, and each one is only given two se'ah.

**The law of a roof adjacent to a public domain. 2 sections:** A roof adjacent to a public domain — within ten handbreadths and above ten handbreadths relative to a courtyard — since the public makes use of it, it is treated like a public domain, and the owner of the roof is forbidden to make use of it from his courtyard unless he makes a fixed ladder from his courtyard. What is a fixed ladder? Any ladder that is fixed there both for weekdays and for Shabbat.

A courtyard that was breached along its entire width or more than ten handbreadths into a public domain — the place of the former wall is treated like the sides of a public domain, which has the status of a karmelit, as does the courtyard itself. If it was breached at a corner, even less than ten handbreadths is forbidden. Similarly a house that was breached at a corner even less than ten handbreadths, and the roof was also breached until only a diagonal strip remains, is forbidden. But a breach that is not at a corner — we apply the principle that the edge of the roof descends and seals, even if the breach is more than ten handbreadths, provided the edge of the roof is not slanted, since then there is no effective edge. Rema: Some say we also require the roof to be four handbreadths wide. (Tosafot and Rosh, ch. Keitzad Mishtatfim, Semag, and Tur) We apply the principle that the edge of the roof descends and seals even with two walls, if there are two complete walls joined together — but two walls facing each other, no. (Tur)

**Which partition is called a partition for carrying. 12 sections:** Any partition that was not made to dwell inside it, but rather for privacy, or to guard what is placed inside it, or to sit in it in order to guard fields — it is a valid partition for carrying within it, but it does not make what is inside it an enclosed dwelling (mukaf l'dirah) if it is more than two se'ah. Therefore, a tree whose branches hang down — if they are not three handbreadths above the ground, and their base where they connect to the tree is ten handbreadths high — it is considered a partition and one may carry throughout it, provided one fills the airspace between the branches with wood or straw and ties the branches so the wind does not move them, for any partition that cannot withstand an ordinary wind is not a valid partition. This applies only up to two se'ah, but more than two se'ah is not valid, even if the tree was planted for this purpose, since it is not made to dwell inside but to sit in its shade to guard the fields.
A mound that is five handbreadths high, and one completed it to ten by making a partition five handbreadths high on top of it — it is considered a valid partition for carrying and for all purposes.

A partition that stands on its own — meaning one not made for the purpose of being a partition — is valid. A partition made on Shabbat is valid, and this applies when it was made unintentionally (shogeg), but if done intentionally (meizid) it is a partition only to be stringent — to make one liable for throwing from a public domain into it — but not to permit carrying within it. This applies when there was no partition there previously; but if there was one, it was removed, and then re-formed, even intentionally, it reverts to its original permitted status. For example, two or three people who surrounded themselves with mats in a public domain and also divided between themselves with mats and made an eruv together — they are permitted to carry from one area to the other. If the mats were rolled up, it became forbidden; if they were spread out again, even intentionally, they revert to their original permitted status.

One may carry throughout a boat, even if it is more than two se'ah, since it is considered enclosed for dwelling (see above Siman 366 and end of Siman 382). If it was turned upside down to dwell beneath it, it constitutes a private domain (reshut hayachid) even on top of it. If it was turned upside down to caulk it (l'zofta), one may only carry within four cubits if it is larger than two se'ah.

One may make a partition with any material — with vessels, with saddles — whether using only horizontal elements (erev) such as ropes, or only vertical elements (shti) such as reeds stuck in the ground. These are permitted up to two se'ah, even for an individual in a settled area, provided there is not a gap of three handbreadths between one rope and another or between one reed and another. This applies even with animals, provided they are tied; and even with people standing next to each other less than three handbreadths apart — even when walking they are considered a partition and the space between them is a private domain — provided they do not know they were positioned to serve as a partition. If even one of them knows, it is forbidden. And even if one did not inform them that he is now making partitions, if it is likely they would find out — such as if he once already made a partition from them — he may not do so again.
If they came initially without knowledge, even if they later became aware, there is no concern.

Some say that the person who wishes to use this partition should not position the people himself, but rather another person should position them without their knowledge. Rema: One should only make a partition of people in a time of need and pressing circumstance. If one forgot something in a public domain, it is preferable to send children to bring the object without a partition than to make a partition of people and have an adult bring it. (Beit Yosef in the name of Shibolei HaLeket, Semag, and Sefer HaIttur)
If the open space exceeds the standing space, it is forbidden, unless each individual gap is less than three handbreadths.

If the open space equals the standing space, it is permitted, whether in vertical or horizontal elements, provided no single opening is more than ten cubits. Up to ten cubits is permitted because it is like a doorway.

If one made a tzurat hapetach, even for a breach wider than ten cubits it is permitted, even if one only planted four posts in four directions and made a tzurat hapetach over them. This applies in a courtyard or alleyway that has residents; but in an open field it does not help in all directions through a tzurat hapetach. According to the Rambam, a tzurat hapetach does not help for a breach wider than ten cubits unless the standing space exceeds the open space. (In that case it helps even in an open field in all directions.) (Beit Yosef in the name of Semag and Semak)

What constitutes a tzurat hapetach? A reed on this side and a reed on that side, and a reed on top of them — even if the top reed does not touch them but there are several cubits between them — provided the side reeds are ten handbreadths high and are aligned directly below the upper reed. If one attached the upper reed to both side reeds or to one of them from the side, it is not valid. The side reeds must be sturdy enough to hold even the smallest door, even one of straw or reeds; but the reed on top need only be any size at all, and even a rush (gemi) is valid.
An arch (meaning a gate made in an arch shape. Rashi) if its legs, meaning before it begins to curve, are ten handbreadths high, it is permitted as a tzurat hapetach.

**Laws of an Alleyway (*Mavoi*) and a Side-Post (*Lechi*) — 36 Sections A place that has three walls — the Sages forbade carrying within it until some corrective arrangement is made on the fourth side.

A courtyard that was breached across its full width up to ten cubits may be rectified with a post four handbreadths wide placed on one side at the breach. If one wishes to rectify it with posts on both sides of the breach, two posts of any minimal width suffice. The same applies if a fourth wall remains standing, measuring four handbreadths in one place, or if one handbreadth remains on each side. All of this must be at a height of ten handbreadths. Even if the breach is less than four handbreadths wide, since it spans the full width it still requires rectification until it is less than three handbreadths. If the breach exceeds ten cubits, even if it does not span the full width, it must be rectified with a doorframe shape (*tzurat hapetach*).

An alleyway that has three walls and is open on the fourth side may be permitted by a side-post (*lechi*) — meaning, as Targum translates, "one board" (*lucha chada*) — of any thickness and width, placed at the entrance of the alleyway, at least ten handbreadths high. It may be made of any material, even a living creature, provided it is tied there with ropes to the walls of the alleyway by pegs projecting from the walls, in such a way that it cannot lie down and thereby be reduced below ten handbreadths. Even if a person is tied there, it also constitutes a lechi.
**4.** If there is some wall on the fourth side, it counts as a lechi, provided it is at least one handbreadth wide.
**5.** A lechi that would be blown over by the wind does not count as a lechi.
**6.** The lechi must not be more than three handbreadths away from the wall.

**7.** Even broken pieces, and pieces of broken pieces, are valid for a lechi. Therefore, one may make a lechi from plaster spread on a wall, provided one takes care that it not be smeared away to less than three handbreadths from the ground.
**8.** A lechi made from the wood of an *asherah* (idolatrous tree) is valid.

**9.** Whether the projection of the lechi is visible to those standing inside the alleyway but not to those standing outside, or visible to those outside facing the alleyway opening but not to those inside — it is valid.

**10.** If it was placed three handbreadths from the wall, or raised three handbreadths from the ground, it is invalid. But if it was raised less than three handbreadths from the ground, even if it is only seven handbreadths and a hairsbreadth high, it is valid.

**11.** Even if it was not placed there as a lechi but happened to be there on its own, it is valid — provided one relied on it before Shabbat. But if one did not rely on it before Shabbat — for instance, there was another lechi and it fell on Shabbat and now one wishes to rely on this one — no. (But if there was no other lechi there before Shabbat, it is as if one had relied on it.)

**12.** A lechi that stands on its own — even if one relied on it before Shabbat — if the alleyway is wider than eight cubits and the lechi protrudes four cubits into it, it is not treated as a lechi and another lechi is needed; it should be placed on the opposite side. If one wishes to place it alongside the first, one should make it slightly thicker or thinner than the protrusion, so that it is recognizable as a lechi. But if it was explicitly placed as a lechi — which is publicly known that a lechi was made for this alleyway — even if it protrudes four cubits it is valid as a lechi.

**13.** A lechi drawn along the wall of the alleyway with its edge placed against the wall's thickness — flush on the inside but visible from the outside, such that the lechi's edge does not cover the full thickness of the wall — if the alleyway is less than four cubits wide it is treated as a lechi, and one may use the wall with its inner edge. If four cubits or more, it is treated as part of the alleyway and it is forbidden to use the entire alleyway since there is effectively no lechi.

**14.** There is another valid arrangement for an alleyway open on the fourth side: a beam (*korah*) placed on top of the alleyway. It must rest on the alleyway wall. But if two pegs were driven outside the alleyway — even right next to it — and the beam was placed on them, it is invalid.
**15.** The beam must be placed with the intent to permit the alleyway. But if it was not made for that purpose, even if one relied on it before Shabbat, it is invalid.

**16.** The beam we mentioned must have a minimum size. Therefore, if it was made from the wood of an *asherah* it is invalid, since it is destined for burning its measurement is considered nullified (*ketutei mechtat shiureih*).

**17.** The required width of the beam is one handbreadth, and its thickness may be any amount, provided it is strong enough to hold a half-brick (*arich*), which is three handbreadths. If it is four handbreadths wide, it need not be strong enough to hold a half-brick.

**18.** Regarding supports — if the beam rests on pegs projecting from the wall that are not a handbreadth wide nor three handbreadths long: some say the pegs must be strong enough to hold both the beam and a half-brick; others say they need only be strong enough to hold the beam alone.
**19.** If the beam is round, its circumference must be at least three handbreadths, which gives it a width of one handbreadth.

**20.** If the beam is curved and the curve bends outside the alleyway, or above twenty handbreadths, or below ten handbreadths: we consider whether, if the curvature were removed, the gap between the two ends would be less than three handbreadths — if so, it is valid; if not, invalid.

**21.** If the beam extends from one wall but does not reach the other — for instance, it rests on poles — or if there are two beams, one extending from one wall and one from the other, meeting in the middle: if the gap between them is less than three handbreadths, valid; if three handbreadths or more, invalid.

**22.** If two beams are placed side by side, neither wide enough alone to hold a half-brick, but together wide enough — i.e., totaling one handbreadth — and with less than three handbreadths between them, no additional beam is needed. If not, another beam must be brought. Some say they must be within one handbreadth of each other.

**23.** If one beam is higher and one is lower, we consider the upper one as if it were lower and the lower one as if it were higher — provided the upper one is not above twenty handbreadths, the lower not below ten, and there are not three handbreadths between them either vertically or horizontally when we consider them as having shifted to be side by side. Some rule this invalid.

**24.** If a mat was spread over the beam but does not reach the ground: if it is three handbreadths above the ground it is invalid, since the beam is covered and no longer visible as a beam, and it is not a partition either since it is three handbreadths off the ground. But if a wide beam was placed and extends a little below ten handbreadths, it is valid.

**25.** If two bent pegs were driven into the two walls of the alleyway, curving inward, and the beam was placed on them — and the pegs are not a handbreadth wide (which would make them count as a beam): if they are not three handbreadths higher than the walls and their bend does not extend three handbreadths, it is valid, since we consider them as if they were flush with the wall tops. If they are three handbreadths higher or their bend is three handbreadths, it is invalid.

**26.** The ruling that an alleyway is permitted by a lechi or beam applies only when its height is not less than ten full handbreadths, its width is no more than ten precise cubits, and its length is at least four full cubits. If any of these conditions is lacking, it can only be rectified with a doorframe shape. If the inner height exceeds twenty precise cubits, it cannot be rectified by a beam, but can be rectified by a lechi. If one wishes to rectify it with a beam, a decorative marking or design must be made on it — one marking on the wall in plaster or on the face of the beam — so that everyone looks at it. If the height exceeds twenty cubits and a structure is built beneath the beam to reduce it below twenty, a structure one handbreadth wide along the width of the beam suffices. But if the height is less than ten handbreadths and one carves into the ground to complete ten, one must carve four cubits into the alleyway across its full width. An alleyway is not permitted by a lechi or beam unless two courtyards open into it and each courtyard has two houses. (Even if all the courtyards open into each other.) Some disagree with this. Each entrance must be at least four handbreadths wide. There must be residents eating in each house, since the location of the bread determines the eruv. Even if one house belongs to a father and one to a son, and the son receives his meals from his father's table yet eats in his own house, they are considered as two. Even if one side has a non-Jew and one a Jew, this is sufficient. Furthermore, the length of the alleyway must exceed its width. If any of these conditions is lacking, it can only be rectified with a four-handbreadth post, two minimal posts on either side, or a doorframe shape. Some say the custom today is to rectify all alleyways with a doorframe shape, since all our alleyways have the status of courtyards. The widespread custom in these lands is to rectify them with a rope tied across the width of the alleyway. This rope does not have the status of a beam since it is not a handbreadth wide, but it works as a doorframe shape, which is valid even with reed at the top, as explained above at the end of Siman 362. Therefore one should be careful to place two poles ten handbreadths high directly beneath the rope, which then works even for a passage open on both ends (*mavoi mefulash*) as a doorframe shape, or even in a courtyard or wherever a doorframe shape works, as explained at the end of Siman 362.

**27.** A courtyard whose length exceeds its width has the status of an alleyway and may be permitted with a lechi or beam. Even if no courtyards and houses open into it, since it is not adjacent to a public domain but opens to an alleyway which opens to the public domain.

**28.** An alleyway less than three handbreadths wide requires no corrective arrangement at all, as it is considered sealed. Some say that any alleyway less than four handbreadths wide requires no arrangement.

**29.** An alleyway whose one side ends at the sea and whose other side ends at a public refuse heap requires nothing, since a public refuse heap is not expected to be cleared away, and we do not worry that the sea will deposit silt (*shirton* — a dry patch like an island from which the water receded and which becomes fit for planting). Some disagree and hold that we do worry that silt may rise and there would be no partition.

**30.** An alleyway with one long side and one short side — even if the long side does not exceed the short by four cubits — the beam is placed only opposite the short side. But if one wishes, a doorframe shape may be made diagonally, and the beam inside the alleyway may also be placed diagonally, so that one uses the short side opposite the short and the long side opposite the long.

**31.** If a lechi was placed in the middle of an alleyway, and there is a courtyard from the lechi outward, and those on the outside also placed a lechi at the head of the alleyway, they restrict one another and must make a joint eruv. If there is no courtyard, or there is a courtyard but the outsiders did not place a lechi at the alleyway head, those from the lechi inward are permitted and those outward are forbidden. But if two posts or a four-handbreadth post was placed in the middle — if the alleyway is no wider than ten cubits — or a doorframe shape was made — if wider than ten cubits — then even if there is a courtyard from the arrangement outward and the outsiders also made an arrangement at the alleyway head, each may make their own eruv and be permitted in their section.

**32.** Just as we ruled that a lechi may be placed in the middle of an alleyway, the same applies to placing a beam in the middle. All of this applies where the inner section has the proper status of an alleyway — its length not less than four cubits, its length exceeding its width, and houses and courtyards opening into it. If not, two minimal posts on either side, or one four-handbreadth post on one side, is required.

**33.** An alleyway twenty cubits wide may be rectified by placing a four-cubit-wide post in the middle, making each side of the post a separate alleyway — since the post's length is four cubits — and a beam is placed at the head of each. Care must be taken that the beam rests on the post or within three handbreadths of it. Each of the two alleyways created by the post must have houses and courtyards opening into it and satisfy all alleyway conditions. The area between the post and the middle wall of the alleyway has the status of a bent alleyway (*mavoi akum*), since these two alleyways curve and are open at both ends to a public domain. Some say it has the status of a bent alleyway only if the distance from the post to the middle wall exceeds ten cubits.

**34.** There is another way to rectify an alleyway twenty cubits wide: set back two cubits from the wall and place a three-cubit post, and do the same on the other side, leaving an opening of ten cubits. Alternatively, set back one cubit and place a post of one and a half cubits, then set back another cubit and place another post of one and a half cubits, doing the same on the other side. Or set back two cubits and two handbreadths and place a post of two cubits and four handbreadths, likewise on the other side. Similar arrangements work — provided the post is wider than the gap between it and the wall, for otherwise the air space on both sides would nullify it. Care must be taken not to leave a large opening while entering through a small one, for if this is done the alleyway's correction is nullified — unless a doorframe shape is made for the smaller opening.

**35.** The post used to reduce the alleyway's width need not be one solid post; reed by reed with gaps of less than three handbreadths suffices, since less than three handbreadths is treated as solid.

**36.** An alleyway that is level inside but slopes (*midrón*) down to the public domain, or is level with the public domain and slopes down inside — if the slope rises ten handbreadths within four cubits, it is treated as if it were entirely vertical and requires no corrective arrangement. (In this case, the mound counts as a partition.)

Laws of a Pass-Through Alleyway and One Shaped Like the Letter Nun — 5 Sections A pass-through alleyway open at both ends to a public domain, or with one side opening to a public domain and the other to a karmelit — or with both ends opening to a karmelit requires a doorframe shape on one side and a lechi or beam on the other. But if one side opens to a public domain and the other to an uneruvated courtyard, only a lechi or beam is needed at each of the two ends. All of this is subject to the conditions explained above in Siman 363, section 27, regarding the laws of an alleyway. But if it is entirely within a courtyard, it requires the courtyard arrangement on both sides.

A public domain itself can only be rectified with doors, and they must be locked at night. Some say that even if they are not locked, they must at least be fit to be locked — so if they are sunken in the ground, one clears them and fixes them so they are fit to be locked. Once the door arrangement is made, the entire area is considered a single courtyard and its alleyways require no further arrangement.

A bent alleyway shaped like the letter dalet is treated as if it were a pass-through alleyway at the bend, and requires a doorframe shape at the bend. At each of its two ends it needs either a lechi, beam, or doorframe shape — and a lechi or beam at the bend. If it is shaped like the letter chet, it requires a doorframe shape at each of its two bends, and a lechi or beam at each of its two ends.

Alleyways that open into one another — when the bend of one of them does not face the public domain — since the outer alleyway opens to the public domain, the alleyway that opens into it at its bend is considered as if it opens to the public domain. And so too the alleyway that opens into that one, and so on for all of them.

An alleyway shaped like the letter nun meaning a large alleyway into which many small alleyways open, with the other ends of the small ones opening to the public domain — even if the openings of the small alleyways on each side do not directly face one another: one makes a doorframe shape for each small alleyway at the point where it opens into the large alleyway, and a lechi or beam at its other end which opens to the public domain. As for the large alleyway itself: if it is a pass-through, one makes a doorframe shape on one side and a lechi or beam on the other; if it is closed at one end, one makes a lechi or beam at its open end.

**Laws of an Alleyway That Was Breached. Contianing 8 Sections** An alleyway that was breached on its side toward its end — if a post four handbreadths wide remains at its end, it is permitted, provided the breach does not exceed ten handbreadths. If no four-handbreadth post remains, it is forbidden unless the breach is less than three handbreadths.

An alleyway breached on its side not toward its end — the maximum is ten handbreadths, even if nothing remains of the wall at the base. (But if many people pass through it, even a breach of only four handbreadths must be rectified there.)

An alleyway breached across its full width into a courtyard, and the courtyard is breached on its other side toward a public domain — if the courtyard residents did not make an eruv with the alleyway residents, the courtyard is permitted, even if the breach faces the alleyway's breach and even if many people pass through it, provided it is no more than ten handbreadths. The alleyway is forbidden even if it does not face the courtyard's breach, since not having made an eruv with the alleyway restricts it — this applies when the alleyway walls extend into the courtyard such that the remaining side-sections within the courtyard are not visible to one standing in the alleyway. But if they are visible, they count as a lechi and it is permitted. If the courtyard residents did make an eruv with the alleyway residents, and the breach from the alleyway into the courtyard is not on the courtyard's side, and the courtyard's breach on the other side does not face the alleyway's breach, and the courtyard belongs to many — the alleyway is also permitted. But if they did not make an eruv, or even if they did but the courtyard's breach toward the alleyway is on its side, or even in the middle of the courtyard and the courtyard's breach on the other side faces it, or even does not face it but the courtyard belongs to a single individual — it is forbidden. If the breach opens into an area smaller than two *se'ah*, or larger but enclosed for dwelling purposes, it is treated as a breach into a courtyard. But if it is larger than two *se'ah* and not enclosed for dwelling, it is as if it opened into a *karmelit* and requires rectification.

One may use the space beneath the beam and opposite the lechi. This applies when the alleyway opens to a public domain, but when it opens to a *karmelit*, it is forbidden both beneath the beam and opposite the lechi, since it combines with the adjacent *karmelit* — like finds like and is stirred.

Although use beneath the beam is permitted, a person should not sit at the entrance of the alleyway with an object in hand, lest the object roll from his hand into the public domain and he bring it back, since there is no visible distinction between his position and the public domain. But at the entrance of a courtyard it is permitted, whether it opens to a public domain or a *karmelit*, since there is a recognizable distinction there.
Women sitting at the entrance of an alleyway with their jugs in hand — one does not protest against them, since this is a rabbinic matter and it is better they sin unknowingly than deliberately.

An alleyway whose beams or lechis fell on Shabbat — even though it was permitted for part of Shabbat, it is forbidden from that point onward, whether it opens to a public domain or a karmelit. Some say this applies only in a city not surrounded by a wall, but in a walled city it remains permitted. Rema: One may rely on this to be lenient. All of this applies when the arrangement was fit to stand the entire Shabbat, but if it was already intended to be demolished from before Shabbat, it is forbidden once it collapses. If there is doubt whether it collapsed before Shabbat or not, we rule leniently.

An alleyway in which a partnership eruv was made and the beam broke — the courtyard in which the eruv is kept, and the courtyards that open into it, are permitted. But courtyards that do not open into that courtyard are forbidden.

About a courtyard with many houses that open up into it, the Rabbis prohibited carrying from house to house until they create an eruv in which they have collected bread from each household and place it in one of the houses in the courtyard. With this method, we see that it's as if all citizens [of the courtyard] are living in one house and the entire courtyard is designated to that one house.

One must place the entire eruv into one vessel, and if they divided it and placed it into two vessels, it is not the case of an eruv unless the first vessel became full, and thus it is permitted. And this is only a case when the two vessels are in one house.

We do not make an eruv with a slice, even if it’s very big. But with a full loaf, even if it’s very small, we make an eruv provided that it will contain the amount of a legal measure. However, if it is taken from it for the sake of a baker’s challah, which is 1/48th, we make an eruv with it, even if it wasn’t set aside for challah. And if it was cut and one fastened it with a toothpick, that he put one end inside the loaf and the second end inside the slice, if it is not recognizable that it was cut, we make an eruv with it. Rama: And there are those who interpreted this that we only make an eruv with a full loaf, that is that all of the eruv together will be [one] whole loaf. Therefore, it is the common practice to gather from every house a little bit of flour and make one full challah and make an eruv with it. And thus, the custom is widespread in all of these provinces. But, one needs to be careful that the challah contain a legal measure’s worth as explained earlier in 358. And even if there are left [homeowners] from [donating] the flour so that the challah is not made from everyone, even so, it is an eruv since one who grants [ownership] to all does not diminish from these people [so that they count]. And this was the intent of those who gave their flour from the outset. So it appears to me.

Friends who were reclining to eat and the day became holy upon them, the bread that is on their table, they may rely on it for an eruv. But this is only when they are reclining in a house, which is fitting to put an eruv there, but in a courtyard, no. (And this is also the law: if they have bread for a shutafut in one of the houses, they can rely on it for the sake of eruv.)
...One should bless on the mitzvah of creating an Eiruv

**Laws of When the Eruv Becomes Invalidated After It Was Made — 5 Sections** If an eruv was made and afterward became invalidated, and one of the courtyard residents comes to fix it again — if he comes to make the eruv from the same type of food as the first, even if the original is completely gone, he need not inform the others, and he may even make the eruv on their behalf using their food. If he comes to make it from a different type of food: if the original is completely gone, he must inform them if he is using their food, but if he is using his own he need not inform them at all. If the original has not completely gone but merely diminished, even if he is using their food he need not inform them.
If new residents were added to the courtyard — if a house opens to two courtyards, he must inform them, since perhaps they do not wish to make an eruv with these others.

What is the minimum amount required for an eruv at the outset? When there are eighteen or fewer participants, the amount is a dried fig's worth per person. If there are more than eighteen — even a thousand or more — the amount is two meals' worth, which is eighteen dried figs, equivalent to six eggs. Some say it is equivalent to eight eggs.
If the eruv was reduced below the minimum amount after the first Shabbat began, and any amount at all remains, it is valid for all subsequent Shabbatot as well.

If the eruv bread became moldy and unfit to eat, it is as if it were completely gone and the eruv must be remade. Rema: Therefore the custom developed to make the eruv from matzah, which does not mold quickly, and furthermore it can be kept through Passover and used as the eruv all year long. This is better than making a new eruv each Shabbat, lest people forget to make one. However, if one wishes to make a new eruv each Shabbat eve and eat the eruv each Shabbat, one may do so. See below Siman 394.

**Laws of Partnership in an Eruv — 8 Sections** One who lives in a gatehouse, portico, or balcony of a courtyard does not restrict the courtyard residents, since these are not considered proper dwellings. But one who lives in a straw house, woodshed, cattle barn, or storehouse does restrict them.

A homeowner who has many houses in a courtyard and lent or rented them to others — if he has in each of them items that cannot be moved on Shabbat due to their weight or due to prohibition (meaning things forbidden to move even for the sake of their place) — the residents of those houses do not restrict him, since they are all considered like guests in his home. Therefore they too are permitted to carry from their houses to the courtyard even without giving an eruv. But if the houses do not belong to him — neither owned nor rented — even if he has items in them that are forbidden to move, they restrict one another. Rema: Some say all this applies when there are no other residents in the courtyard besides them, but when there are other residents who bring their eruv to them, each one must make an eruv. One who rented a large building from a non-Jew and sublet one of its units to another — if he did not originally rent it with that intention, it is as if the entire building is his and he merely rented one of the houses to another. But if he originally rented it with that intention, it is as if there are two houses and it does not help, even if one of them has a hold in the other's house.

Five groups who spent Shabbat in a large hall and divided it with partitions — if they all pass through one another's sections since there is only one opening to the courtyard, through the outermost section, and all pass through it — only the two innermost need contribute to the eruv, and all the others are considered a gatehouse for them. If each one has an opening to the courtyard — Rema: or they do not pass through one another but each has an opening to a gatehouse in front of them and the gatehouse opens to the courtyard — if the partitions reach the ceiling or come within three handbreadths of it, making each one a separate room even if they are made of curtains: if the courtyard residents place the eruv in one of the other courtyard houses, each and every group in the hall must contribute an eruv. But if they placed the eruv in this hall, none of them need contribute an eruv since they all dwell in this house, and the house in which the eruv is placed need not contribute. Similarly, if there are no other residents in the courtyard, they need no eruv. If they divided it with partitions that do not reach the ceiling — even if the courtyard residents place their eruv in one of the other courtyard houses — one eruv suffices for all five groups. Rema: If some made partitions and some did not — those who made them are considered separate, and those who did not are considered joint. If there are residents in actual upper stories, even if the courtyard residents placed the eruv in the hall, each group must contribute an eruv. But one who has a tutor or scribe in his house, and likewise students learning before their teacher and living in his house each in their own room — even if each has an opening to the courtyard and eats and sleeps in their room — they do not restrict.

Courtyard residents who all eat at one table — even if each has their own house — need no eruv since they are like members of one household. If they need to make an eruv with residents of another courtyard, they bring only one eruv and one loaf to the place with which they are making the eruv. If the eruv comes to them, they need not contribute an eruv, just as the house in which the eruv is placed need not contribute, since all these houses are considered as one. Rema: Similarly, if many homeowners eat in one room each at their own table, even if each sleeps in their own room, one eruv suffices for all, since there is no partition separating their eating area — this is like five who spent Shabbat in a hall, etc. Even if they sometimes draw a curtain before them for privacy, it is not considered a partition since it is not there permanently.

One who eats in one place and sleeps in another — his eating place is primary and that is where he creates a restriction. Therefore brothers who eat in their father's house and sleep in their own houses do not restrict. But if he gives them portions and they eat in their own houses, they do restrict. This applies when the other courtyard residents place their eruv elsewhere, but if the other courtyard residents place their eruv in one of these houses, or if there are no other residents with them in the courtyard, they need not make an eruv.

One who has five wives and five slaves who receive their portions from him and each eats in their own house, and likewise a student who receives portions from his teacher and eats in his own house — they do not restrict one another if there are no other residents with them in the courtyard, or if the eruv comes to them.

Ten houses one inside the other, all passing through one another and exiting through the outermost to the courtyard — only the two innermost need contribute to the eruv, and the rest are exempt since they are all considered a gatehouse.

A guest in a courtyard — even if staying in their own house — if not staying permanently but for thirty days or fewer, does not restrict the courtyard residents, and both he and they are permitted in his house and in theirs. Rema: Even if the guests are many and the host is one — but this specifically requires one established host, for then the guests are nullified relative to him. But guests together restrict one another immediately. See below at the end of Siman 391. And regarding a non-Jewish guest, see above Siman 384.

**When One of the Courtyard Residents Leaves or Dies — 6 Sections** One of the courtyard residents who left his house and went to spend Shabbat in another courtyard — even one adjacent to his own — if he put it out of his mind and does not intend to return to his house on Shabbat, he does not restrict them. This applies to a Jew, but a non-Jew — even if he went to spend Shabbat in another city — still restricts them until they rent his place from him, if it is within one day's journey, since it is possible he may come on Shabbat. But if it is further away, he does not restrict. Some say that a non-Jew too, if he went to spend Shabbat in another courtyard, does not restrict. [And this appears to be the primary ruling] [And if the non-Jew does come on Shabbat, see above Siman 383]
A Jewish courtyard resident who went to spend Shabbat in another courtyard and did not intend to return on Shabbat — but then changed his mind on Shabbat and returned — does not restrict.

An outsider who had a house in the courtyard and died, leaving his domain to one of the courtyard residents — if he died while it was still day, the inheritor does not restrict, since the eruv he made covers his own house and also permits what he inherited. But if he died after nightfall, he restricts, and even though the inheritor had made an eruv with them, it does not help for what he inherited afterward on Shabbat.

One of the courtyard residents who died on Shabbat — if he had made an eruv, even if an outsider inherits from him, he does not restrict. If he had not made an eruv: if an outsider inherits from him, as long as the outsider does not come to live with them he does not restrict; if he comes to live on Shabbat in the house of his benefactor, he restricts. If one of the courtyard residents inherits from him — if the inheritor had made an eruv and was living together with the deceased in his house, he does not restrict even though the deceased had not made an eruv. But if he was not living with the deceased but in another house in the courtyard, he restricts even though the inheritor had made an eruv, since the deceased had not made an eruv. If the deceased died while it was still day and an outsider inherits from him, the outsider restricts — provided he comes to the deceased's house on Shabbat.

A Jew and a convert who were living in a courtyard, and the convert died while it was still day and a Jew took possession of his property — even if he did not take possession until after nightfall, he restricts until he renounces his domain like any other inheritor. If the convert died after nightfall, the one who took possession does not restrict, since the original permitted status remains in force.

One of the courtyard residents who was dying — even though he cannot survive the day — he restricts until bread is acquired on his behalf and an eruv is made for him. Similarly, a minor restricts even though he cannot eat an olive's worth. But a guest does not restrict, as explained in Siman 370.

**The laws of apartment partners regarding an Eruv. Containing 19 aragraphs:** Roofs, courtyards, and enclosed yards are all considered one domain with respect to utensils that were in them when Shabbat began. It is therefore permitted to carry such items from one to another—even if they belong to different owners who did not join in an eruv. One may carry from one courtyard to another, to a roof, to the top of a wall between them, and from one roof to another adjacent roof—even if the other is much higher. One may also carry from a roof to a karpaf not larger than two se’ah, or one that was enclosed for dwelling even if larger, or to an alleyway (mavoy) that has been properly prepared with a side-post (lechi) or beam (korah), even if no eruv was made there. Even though the residents of a courtyard made an eruv among themselves—since household items are commonly found in the courtyard—it is nevertheless permitted to carry utensils that were in this courtyard at the onset of Shabbat to another courtyard, and we are not concerned lest one carry items that were in the house to another courtyard, roof, or karpaf.

A karpaf larger than two se’ah that was not enclosed for dwelling has the status of a karmelit, and it is forbidden to carry from it to another karpaf—bringing in or taking out—except for four cubits total (two cubits in each).

Two courtyards that wish to make a joint eruv to permit even items that were in houses do not need a new eruv. Rather, the eruv they already made may be taken by one resident on behalf of all and placed in one of the houses of the second courtyard. If he wishes, he may even bring his own bread there, and then all are permitted. <smal>Rema: This applies provided the residents of his courtyard first joined with him (Responsa of the Rosh §16), or they are not required to make an eruv as explained in Siman 370 (Beit Yosef). And provided the residents of the second courtyard made their own eruv; they do not need additional bread, as their existing eruv suffices.

Two courtyards cannot join in one eruv unless there is a doorway between them, or a window measuring four by four handbreadths, with part of it within ten handbreadths of the ground. If so, they may choose to make one joint eruv or each separately (see below Siman 386:2 regarding Israelites dwelling in two or three places).

A window between two houses, even if above ten handbreadths, if they wish, they may join together in an eruv. The same applies to a skylight between a house and an upper story—even above ten handbreadths—they may join, even if there is no ladder. </smallrema:>

A house situated between two courtyards and open to both, and it joined in an eruv with both—but the courtyards did not join with each other—one may not carry items that were in houses from one courtyard to the other via that house. If there is a wall between two courtyards ten handbreadths high, or if the ground of one courtyard is five handbreadths higher and a five-handbreadth partition was built to complete ten, they cannot join in one eruv. If the wall is ten high for both and produce is on top, the residents of both courtyards may lower it into their courtyards and raise produce that was in the courtyards onto it, and lower it into the other courtyard—whether the wall is four handbreadths wide or not. But produce that was in a house: if the wall is four wide, it is forbidden to raise or lower it; if not four wide, it is permitted (provided they do not exchange items, as above Siman 346:1). If the wall is ten high for one courtyard but not the other (e.g., one ground is higher), the one for whom it is not ten high may use it even with house-items; the other may not use it even with courtyard-items—provided the wall is four wide. If not four wide, both may use it even for house-items, even if each made its own eruv.

If the wall was breached up to ten cubits, it is considered like a doorway—provided it was not completely breached. If breached more than ten cubits, it is considered like one courtyard and they must join in one eruv (certainly if there is no ten-high partition at all, they must join) (R. Yonatan Perek Chalon).

If a wall between two courtyards is ten high for both, and a ladder four wide was placed against it, and similarly in the second courtyard—even if the ladders are not directly opposite—if less than three handbreadths apart they are considered like a doorway. If three apart: if the wall is four wide, still considered a doorway; if not, not. This applies to a ladder with four rungs; fewer do not suffice unless its sides and rungs are heavy so its weight fixes it in place. If the wall is only ten high and one erects a ladder seven and a bit high, four wide, adjacent to the wall, it permits use of the wall and joint eruv, since less than three remain to the top. If one removed a section from the top to reduce it below ten: if four wide, effective for doorway and use; if not, ineffective except opposite that place.

If one built a platform at the base of the wall to reduce its height: if four long along the wall and four projecting outward, it permits use of the entire wall but does not count as a doorway unless it reaches the top. If not four by four, it does not help even opposite it.
If one inverted a vessel four by four and any height to reduce the wall below ten, it permits use opposite the reduction—provided it is affixed with mortar.
If one built platform upon platform: if the lower is four by four, or even if not but the upper is four by four and within three handbreadths, it permits use but not joint eruv.

A projection from the wall four by four with any ladder placed on it permits use—provided the lowest rung is within three of the ground and no gap of three between rungs, and the ladder rests atop the projection. If leaned beside it, no. If the wall is under twenty high, one projection in the middle suffices; if twenty high, two are needed—one within the lower ten and one within the upper ten—unless directly opposite each other enabling a ladder.

Two ladders placed side by side without four width, separated to total four, and the space filled with straw—this does not help, since one steps in the middle and cannot climb straw. If the ladder is central and straw on the side, it helps both for use and joint eruv.

If a ladder is not four wide and one carved the wall beside it to complete four, it suffices to carve ten high. If no ladder but one carved rungs into the wall, one must carve the entire height; this helps for both use and joint eruv.

If there is a tree beside the wall used as a ladder, they may join. But if an Asherah tree was used, they may not join, since it is forbidden to climb (as it is prohibited for benefit). The Rosh writes the opposite: a regular tree does not help, but an Asherah does if dry.

A trench between two courtyards ten deep and four wide—they cannot join even if filled with straw unless annulled. If filled with dirt or pebbles—even without explicit annulment—they must join (see Siman 358:2). Rema: Some say that if filled with produce, it is presumed annulled, as people commonly store produce there (Hagahot Ashiri).

If a plank like a bridge is placed from one edge of the trench to the other and is four wide, it is like a doorway—they may join or separate. Rema: The same if filled four wide with something permanently annulled (Beit Yosef). If the plank runs lengthwise four cubits, even minimal width suffices, since it reduced the width from four.
If the trench is ten deep for one but not the other, or equal for both, its law is like that of a wall.

A stack of straw between two courtyards: if ten high, each makes its own eruv. If reduced below ten during the week, they must join. While still ten high, neither may remove straw on Shabbat for his animal—even to place the animal there to eat. But if he can stand before it to prevent it turning elsewhere, that is permitted. According to the Rosh, even during the week one may not remove straw or position the animal by hand. This applies to a stack between courtyards; between two houses, one may feed his animal from it by hand.

**What things present in a courtyard do not restrict. Containing 4 sections** A balcony that serves as a passageway to upper stories opening onto it, standing in the courtyard, accessed by a ladder, with the upper story residents descending from it to the courtyard and passing through to the public domain — they do not restrict the courtyard residents, since a ladder has the status of an opening, making it like two courtyards with an opening between them, where if they wish they may make a joint eruv and if they wish each may make their own eruv — provided all the balcony residents make their own eruv among themselves so that the permitted foot remains in its place.

If they did not make a joint eruv and there is a mound or pillar in the courtyard shared between the two — if they are not ten handbreadths high, they are considered shared between the courtyard and the balcony and both are forbidden to carry there vessels from the houses. If they are ten handbreadths above the courtyard floor and within ten handbreadths of the balcony and within four handbreadths of the balcony — the balcony residents are permitted since using it is more convenient for them than for the courtyard residents. But if they are four handbreadths or more away from the balcony, even though they are ten handbreadths high from the courtyard and within ten handbreadths of the balcony — they are considered shared between the courtyard and the balcony since both can use them by throwing. Therefore both are forbidden to carry there vessels that rested in the houses until they make an eruv.
If there was a platform four handbreadths wide in front of the balcony, the balcony does not restrict the courtyard residents since it is thereby separated from them.

Projections extending from the walls — anything below ten handbreadths is considered part of the courtyard and the courtyard residents may use it. Anything within the upper ten handbreadths adjacent to the upper story — the upper story residents may use it. What remains between the lower ten and the beginning of the upper ten handbreadths — both are forbidden to use it, and neither may use it with vessels that rested in the houses unless they made an eruv.

**Laws of a pit and well between two courtyards. Containing 4 paragraphs** A pit between two courtyards where there is no opening or window through which they could make a joint eruv — or where there is one but they did not make an eruv — one may not draw water from it on Shabbat unless a partition ten hand breadths high was constructed above the waterline. A hand breadth of the partition must descend into the water. If the entire partition is within the water, a hand breadth must protrude above the waterline so that one domain is visibly distinct from the other. Similarly, if a beam four hand breadths wide was placed across the mouth of the pit, one resident draws water from one side of the beam and the other from the opposite side. Rema: This applies specifically when one comes to draw with vessels from the house. But with courtyard vessels, no such arrangement is needed, since courtyards are considered a single domain, as stated above in Siman 372.

A well situated in the middle of a pathway between two courtyard walls — even if it is four handbreadths distant from each wall — both residents may draw from it and need no projections above it, since no person restricts his neighbor through airspace. Rema: This applies specifically when the courtyards do not open into the pathway but only through windows. Some say that if the well is not four handbreadths from each wall, they do restrict one another even in this case.

Two courtyards with three ruins between them: each resident may use the ruin adjacent to his courtyard — through windows, by throwing — and the middle ruin may be used by both. If all three ruins were adjacent to houses such that the middle ruin faced the other two in the arrangement of three points of a tripod, each resident may use the ruin on his own side, but the third ruin — which is close to both courtyards — is forbidden to both.
An outhouse situated between two houses that did not make a joint eruv: both parties have jurisdiction over it and it is therefore forbidden to both. (See also above, Siman 355.)

**Laws of courtyards that open into one another. Contains 5 sections** Three courtyards opening into one another and opening to a public domain, where each of the outer ones made an eruv with the middle one but the outer ones did not make an eruv with each other — the outer ones are forbidden to each other, the middle one is permitted with each of them, and they are permitted with it. This applies when the middle one placed its eruv in one and its eruv in the other, or when the outer ones placed their eruv in the middle one in two separate houses. But if both outer ones placed their eruv in the middle one in one house, all three are permitted with one another.

Two courtyards one inside the other, the inner one opening to the outer one and the outer one to an alleyway, and the inner one has foot traffic through the outer one — if the inner one made an eruv on its own and the outer one did not, or if each made its own eruv and one person from the outer one forgot and did not make an eruv — the inner one is permitted and the outer one is forbidden. If the outer one made an eruv and the inner one did not, or if each made its own eruv and one person from the inner one forgot and did not make an eruv — both are forbidden. If each made its own eruv, each is permitted in its own courtyard.

If they made a joint eruv and placed it in the outer one, and one person — whether from the inner or outer — forgot and did not make an eruv, both are forbidden until he renounces his domain. If they placed their eruv in the inner one and one person from the inner one forgot and did not make an eruv, both are forbidden. But if one person from the outer one forgot and did not make an eruv, the inner one is permitted.

If one individual lives in the inner one and one individual in the outer one, or two in the outer one who made an eruv — the individual in the inner one does not restrict the outer one. Rema: The same applies to many who are like an individual and need not make an eruv, as explained above in Siman 370.

Three courtyards one inside the other with one individual in each — even though many have foot traffic through the outer one, they do not restrict, since each one is permitted in its own place. But if there were two in the inner one who did not make an eruv, they restrict the individuals in the middle and outer ones. This is the general rule: a foot that is forbidden in its own place restricts in other places, but a foot that is permitted in its own place does not restrict in other places.

**Laws of courtyards and houses between them. Contains 2 sections** Two courtyards with three houses between them opening into one another, wishing to make a joint eruv — one courtyard comes through the house adjacent to it and places its eruv in the middle house, and the second courtyard does likewise. They are then permitted in all three, since each house adjacent to a courtyard counts as a gatehouse for it and need not contribute bread, and the middle house is the house in which the eruv is placed and also need not contribute bread.

Two courtyards with two houses between them, where they did not make a joint eruv but each made its own eruv separately — and one came from his courtyard through the house adjacent to it and placed his eruv in the house adjacent to the other courtyard, and the other did likewise, also placing his eruv in the house adjacent to the first courtyard — they have not acquired an eruv, since each one placed their eruv in the gatehouse of the other courtyard.

**Laws of renouncing domain. Contains 4 paragraphs:** One of the courtyard residents who forgot and did not make an eruv with the others restricts them. What is their remedy? He renounces his domain to them by saying "my domain is renounced to you" or "transferred to you," and no formal acquisition is required. He may renounce even after nightfall. If he lives with four or five others he must renounce to each one individually, saying "my domain is renounced to you and to you." Some say it suffices to say "my domain is renounced to all of you." If he renounced his domain without specification, he has only renounced his share in the courtyard — therefore they are permitted to carry from their houses to the courtyard, and he too is like a mere guest. But they are forbidden to carry from his house to the courtyard, and so is he. Some say he must lock his house so that he not come to carry out in a forbidden manner, and he should only open it when he wishes to enter or exit, locking it immediately after.
If he also renounced to them the domain of his house, both he and they are permitted to carry to the courtyard from his house as well as from their houses.
If he does not wish to renounce his domain to them but rather to rent it — some say this is effective like renunciation, and some say it is not effective.

If the courtyard residents who made an eruv renounce their domain to one who did not make an eruv — he is permitted to carry from his house to the courtyard but not from their houses (unless they explicitly renounced the domain of their houses as well). They are forbidden even from his house to the courtyard, and we do not say they become like guests, since many cannot become guests of an individual. The same applies if there were only two and one renounced to the other — the one who renounced is forbidden even in the other's domain, and the other is permitted even in his own. Similarly, many who did not make an eruv who give their domain to many who did make an eruv — since an individual becomes a guest of the many, but many do not become guests even of many, nor does an individual become a guest of an individual. If two forgot and did not make an eruv, they may renounce their domain — each one renouncing his domain to all the courtyard residents — whether renouncing to the many who made an eruv, provided each one renounces to each individual, or whether renouncing to one who did not make an eruv. But they cannot renounce to two who did not make an eruv — whether the many who made an eruv are renouncing or a single individual who did not make an eruv — since even after they renounce to them, there are still two who restrict one another. Even if one says to the other "I renounce to you on condition that you in turn renounce to your fellow" — this is not effective.

**Laws of one who renounced his domain and then carried anyway. Containing 7 paragraphs:** One who renounced his domain and afterward carried from his house to the courtyard inadvertently does not restrict. If he did so deliberately he restricts, since he thereby retracts his renunciation. But if they had already taken possession meaning they carried from their houses to the courtyard or brought in from the courtyard to their houses he can no longer retract his renunciation. According to Rashi, taking possession is only effective if it occurred after nightfall.

Renunciation of domain applies from courtyard to courtyard as well. Whether two courtyards with an opening between them where each made its own eruv and they did not make a joint eruv — each one may renounce its domain to the other, making it permitted to use it, but not the reverse. Or whether two courtyards one inside the other where only the outer one made an eruv and the inner one restricts the outer — the inner one may renounce its domain to the outer so that it neither uses nor passes through it except when it needs to exit, and the outer one will be permitted. Or if they made a joint eruv and placed it in the outer one and one person from the inner one forgot and did not make an eruv — he may renounce his domain, meaning he renounces to each member of the inner courtyard and to each member of the outer courtyard, leaving only himself forbidden while all the others are permitted.

Renunciation of domain applies in a ruin as well — if there were two houses with a ruin between them belonging to both, and they forgot and did not make an eruv, one may renounce his domain to the other and the other will be permitted in it.

Renunciation of domain applies from house to house — if there were two houses with an opening between them and they did not make an eruv, one may renounce his domain to the other. Even the one who renounced is permitted to carry from his house to his fellow's house, but he cannot carry from his fellow's house to his own house, since that would be reclaiming the domain he renounced. Similarly, if he has a room opening into his house and he renounced the domain of his house, he is forbidden to carry from the room into his house. Rema: Some say one may only renounce from house to house if he retains one room for himself that he did not renounce, in which case he is permitted to bring in even from his fellow's house to his own. It is good to be stringent about this at the outset. (Beit Yosef in the name of Rabbeinu Yerucham, Rabbeinu Tam and Hagahot Maimoni Perek 2 in Hilchot Eiruvin

Two houses on two sides of a public domain that non-Jews enclosed with a partition on Shabbat, creating something like a courtyard to which both houses open, making them restrict one another — they cannot renounce domain to each other.
An inheritor may renounce domain — if the deceased had not made an eruv and died on Shabbat and the inheritor comes to live in the courtyard and restricts, he may renounce his domain.

One may renounce and renounce again — meaning the residents of one courtyard renounce their domain to the residents of another courtyard or to one of its members until they carry out whatever they wish, and then those others renounce back to the first ones until they too carry out whatever they wish.

**Whether a non-Jew's residence invalidates an eruv. Contains 20 sections** One who lives with a non-Jew in a courtyard — the non-Jew does not restrict him until there are two Jews living in two houses who restrict each other, at which point the non-Jew restricts them. It does not help for the non-Jew to renounce his domain; rather they must rent from him. Rema: A Jew who rented or lent his house to a non-Jew does not restrict him, since he did not rent or lend it to him in order to restrict him. But if the house belongs to a non-Jew and a Jew rented it from him and the non-Jew lives in the house with him, the rental of the house does not help regarding the rental for the eruv. A Jew who lent or rented a house to his fellow in a place where non-Jews live — even if he has a hold in the house, it does not help and they must rent from the non-Jew.
If the Jews renounced their domain to one of them in order that he be considered alone relative to the non-Jew, it does not help.

If the non-Jew has no foot traffic over the Jews, he does not restrict — for example, two courtyards opening into each other with no foot traffic between them, where a non-Jew lives in one courtyard and two or more Jews live in the other. They may carry in and out between the courtyards on Shabbat through a window between them and need not rent from the non-Jew.
One who rents from a non-Jew without specification — it is effective and he need not explain that it is to permit carrying, nor does he need to write any document for the rental.
One may rent from a non-Jew even for less than a perutah's worth, and it is permitted to rent from him on Shabbat.
As long as the non-Jew does not retract, the rental is effective even for a long period. (He cannot retract the rental until he returns the money.)
If they rented from the non-Jew for a specified time, when the time expires they must rent again, and they must also make a new eruv, since the first eruv does not automatically resume.
If they rented from the non-Jew for a specified time and within that time the non-Jew rented his dwelling to another, the first rental suffices.
Five people living in one courtyard — one of them rents from the non-Jew on behalf of all of them.
If they rented from him against his will, it is not effective even if he had previously been accustomed to rent.

But from his wife, or from his hired worker or laborer, they may rent even if he objects. (The hired worker of a hired worker, and the laborer of the homeowner, are considered like the homeowner's own hired worker.)

If he is unwilling to rent, one of the courtyard residents should approach him until he lends him his domain — giving him the right to place something there — which makes him like his hired worker or laborer, and he rents without the non-Jew's awareness. Some say he need not rent at all but simply places his eruv there and that suffices.
If he designated a specific place in the house he is lending — since he is not like his agent throughout the entire house, it is not effective.

If they rented from his hired worker or laborer for a specified time — even if he dismissed him as his hired worker or laborer within that time — they are permitted until the time expires. But if they rented from him without specification, once he dismissed him the rental is voided. Rema: The same applies if they rented from the king's treasurer and he was completely dismissed from the king's service. But if he was only removed from the treasury position yet still receives the king's provisions, he is still considered a hired worker or laborer and one may rent from him, and therefore the first rental also remains valid.

If a Jew and a non-Jew live in one house, one must rent from the non-Jew and make an eruv with the Jew. Rema: This applies when each has their own separate dwelling. Similarly, two non-Jews living in the same manner in one house — one must rent from both of them.

If a non-Jew has five Jewish hired workers or laborers living in his house, their dwelling is not considered a proper dwelling such that they would restrict one another. (The rental from a non-Jew does not restrict if one rented from the homeowner.)

Two courtyards one inside the other — a Jew and non-Jew in the inner one and a Jew in the outer one; or a Jew and non-Jew in the outer one and a Jew in the inner one; and even a non-Jew in the inner one and two Jews in the outer one — the non-Jew restricts. Some say that even a non-Jew in the inner one and one Jew in the outer one restricts.

A non-Jew who rented his house to another non-Jew — if the owner retains any hold in the house such that he has the right to place any items there, they may rent from him. If he retains no hold at all: if the landlord can evict the tenant before the rental period expires, they may rent from him; if not, it is not effective unless they rent from the tenant. Rema: Similarly, any individual who has a hold in the house may be rented from, since he is no worse than a hired worker or laborer.

A courtyard in which a Jew and non-Jew live, where one Jew's house is adjacent to the other's and does not open to the courtyard but has windows between them — he cannot make an eruv with him through the window between them in order to carry his vessels through his neighbor's house which opens to the courtyard. But if there is an opening between them, it is permitted. Some say that even if there is an opening between them, it is forbidden.

A courtyard in which a Jew and non-Jew reside, where windows open from one Jew's house to another Jew's house and they made an eruv through the windows — even though they are permitted to carry from house to house through the windows, they are forbidden to carry from house to house through the doors on account of the non-Jew, until they rent from him. Rema: A ship with many Jews on it who have designated quarters must make an eruv and rent domain from the non-Jewish ship owner, or have it included in the ship fare. See above Siman 366, section 2.
